paragraph.text: B11. "You don't live on a farm, so you don't know the truth"

people who live in the countryside know many things city people don't, and they are worth listening to. But the practices under discussion — slaughter age, separating calves, breeding for fast growth, stocking density in sheds — aren't secrets known only to those who live on farms: they are described by the industry itself, in technical manuals, regulations and scientific assessments. And the argument has a bigger problem: it doesn't say anything in the critique is wrong; it only says the critic has no right to speak. Many people who lived and worked on farms reached the same conclusion as vegans.
this chapter is about the appeal to experience. The appeal to technical authority is B8, and the claim that the footage shows exceptions is B10
"Easy to talk from a flat in the city. Come live on a farm, see what it's really like, and then we'll talk."
Knowledge of a practice comes largely from direct experience of it.
People who criticise animal farming have, as a rule, never lived on a farm.
Images and accounts from outside pick the worst cases and don't show everyday life.
So the critique comes from people who don't know the reality, and shouldn't be taken seriously.

P1 is partly true, and P3 points to a real risk in any exposé. P2 is a generalisation that is often false. The central problem is the leap to C, which swaps assessing what is said for assessing who says it.
: even if P1 to P3 were true, the critique could be correct. Knowing whether a claim is true requires examining it, not examining the address of whoever made it.
"You've never even seen a cow up close."
"City people think milk comes from a carton."
"Come work a week on the farm and then tell me."
"Some city vegan trying to teach farmers their job."
"Urban discourse about the rural ignores the situated knowledge of those who live off the land."
"That footage shows exceptions, or it's been manipulated." (which is B10)

People who live in the countryside know lots about plants and animals, and it's good to learn from them. But you don't need to live there to know that a calf cries when it's taken from its mother, or that a chicken lives only a few weeks: the people who raise the animals write that in their own books. And many people who lived in the countryside also thought this was wrong.

What is being criticised isn't a secret of country life. Slaughter age, separating calves, shed stocking density and breeding for fast growth are in the technical manuals, the regulations and the scientific reports of the industry itself. And the argument doesn't say the critique is wrong: it says whoever makes it can't speak. If that held, nobody could have an opinion on anything they don't do every day. Besides, many people who lived and worked on farms reached the same conclusion.
"What exactly did I say that's wrong? If it's that, show me, and I'll change my mind."
The sentence can mean three different things, and only the first deserves an answer on the merits.
Check the fact, and correct it if need be
Say what it is, so it can be examined
Who says something doesn't change whether it's true
The argument almost always arrives in the form of the third row, leaning on the legitimacy of the first.

text.bold: 1. The practices are documented by the industry itself.

paragraph.text: Nobody needs privileged access to know at what age broiler chickens are slaughtered, how calf separation works in dairy, or what density is allowed in a shed. That information is in technical manuals, regulations and scientific assessments, such as the European food safety authority's 2023 opinion on broiler chickens. The critique usually starts from what the industry itself says it does.

text.bold: 2. Attacking the source doesn't refute the content.

paragraph.text: Saying "you live in the city" doesn't show that any claim is false. It is the genetic fallacy, or an attack on the person: who speaks is assessed instead of what is said.

text.bold: 3. The criterion, applied consistently, silences everyone.

paragraph.text: If only those who live a practice could have an opinion on it, nobody could discuss prisons without having been imprisoned, nor child labour without having worked as a child, nor industrial policy without having been a factory worker. And the criterion silences its users too: most people who eat meat have never lived on a farm.

text.bold: 4. Proximity brings knowledge, but also habit.

paragraph.text: Someone who grows up with a practice learns a great deal about it and, at the same time, learns to see it as normal. Familiarity isn't impartiality, and an outside perspective is exactly what allows asking what, from inside, doesn't even look like a question.

text.bold: 5. Many people who lived on farms reached the same conclusion.

paragraph.text: Howard Lyman, a fourth-generation cattle rancher in the United States, went vegan and became a critic of animal agriculture. Initiatives such as the Transfarmation Project, in the United States, support farmers who want to leave intensive animal farming. Living on a farm doesn't, by itself, lead to one conclusion.

text.bold: 6. Experience can be brought into the conversation.

paragraph.text: If people who live in the countryside know something that contradicts the critique, the way to use that knowledge is to say it. The argument doesn't do that: it just declares that the other person doesn't know, without saying what.
Stocking densities above 11 kg/m² increase footpad dermatitis and reduce walking ability; recommends limiting breeds' growth rate

The serious version isn't the attack. It is the observation that the technical, economic and cultural knowledge of people who live off the land is often dismissed in urban debates, and that proposals made without listening to farmers tend to fail and to push the cost onto those with the least.
(e) Why the reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: It asks to include a voice, not to exclude another.

paragraph.text: Listening to people who live off the land is necessary; silencing critics doesn't follow from it.

text.bold: It applies to the transition, not to the moral question.

paragraph.text: Knowing how to change without harming rural families is knowledge farmers have. Knowing whether animals should be killed doesn't depend on where you live (J12).

text.bold: Used well, it strengthens the critique.

paragraph.text: Many of the strongest accounts of what happens on farms come from people who worked on them.

text.bold: The person saying it often doesn't live on a farm either.

paragraph.text: And has opinions about farming with no trouble.

text.bold: They have opinions on many things they don't live.
They accept the account of someone who worked on a farm when it agrees with them.

paragraph.text: And reject it when it doesn't.
"Us in the countryside" against "them in the city" decides before the content
Literature on social identity and in-group bias
Disqualifying the speaker avoids facing what is said
What is seen every day stops looking like a question
The principle under test is: "only those who live off a practice may criticise it".
Only former child workers could criticise it
Only former prisoners could have opinions on the prison system
It would silence journalists, lawyers and researchers
Someone who never lived on a farm couldn't defend animal farming
The criterion silences its users too

It gets something important right: people who live in the countryside have knowledge that urban debates tend to ignore, and critiques made without it often get things wrong. Some animal advocates repeat false or exaggerated claims about animal farming, and that weakens the cause (see
). It also gets right that changes made without listening to rural families tend to fail and to push the cost onto those with the least.

But what is being criticised doesn't depend on living on a farm to be known, and who says something doesn't change whether it's true. The way to use the experience of people who live in the countryside is to bring it into the conversation, not to use it to end it.
